elements.quote: Background: There is limited evidence to evaluate the sustainability of evidence-based interventions (EBIs) for healthcare improvement.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states the current limited state of evidence about evaluating sustainability, identifying an important uncertainty in the field.

elements.quote: Through an integrative review, we aimed to identify approaches to evaluate the sustainability of evidence-based interventions (EBIs) and sustainability outcomes.
elements.reason: The abstract explains the aim and rationale for conducting the review (to identify approaches and outcomes) and situates it within the problem of limited evidence and need to understand sustainability.

elements.quote: A focus on evaluation is what differentiates this review from recent syntheses published on approaches to sustainability research.
elements.reason: The discussion explicitly compares the review to recent syntheses and explains how this review addresses a different/remaining need, justifying the current review relative to existing reviews.

elements.quote: Integrative reviews can include diverse data sources and do not restrict the type of study design. Furthermore, integrative reviews take a more flexible approach to analysis compared to systematic reviews, combining both quantitative and qualitative data if there are similarities [12-14].
elements.reason: The review is an integrative review of evaluation approaches rather than a review of intervention effects; therefore describing a proposed mechanism of action of an intervention is not applicable.

elements.quote: Integrative reviews can include diverse data sources and do not restrict the type of study design. Furthermore, integrative reviews take a more flexible approach to analysis compared to systematic reviews, combining both quantitative and qualitative data if there are similarities [12-14].
elements.reason: The manuscript reviews evaluation approaches for sustainability rather than evaluating a specific complex intervention or its delivery context; thus inclusion of a logic model for a specific intervention is not applicable.

elements.quote: The aim of this integrative review was to identify and synthesize approaches that have been used to evaluate the sustainability of EBIs in healthcare. We aimed to enhance our understanding of sustainability definitions, research designs, data collection methods, timing, measures, and sustainability outcomes used for sustainability evaluation studies.
elements.reason: The review explicitly states clear objectives/aims about identifying and synthesizing approaches and specific aspects (definitions, designs, measures, outcomes). However, the objectives are not presented using a recognised question‑formulation framework (e.g., PICO or similar), so the requirement to state objectives using a relevant framework is not fully met.

elements.quote: Through an integrative review, we aimed to identify approaches to evaluate the sustainability of evidence-based interventions (EBIs) and sustainability outcomes.
elements.reason: This review aims to identify evaluation approaches for sustainability rather than to assess intervention effects or planned comparisons; therefore PICO-style planned comparisons for intervention effects do not apply.

elements.quote: Articles were included if they: • Were published in a peer-review journal • Were primary research • Had explicit research design and data collection methods • Had an explicit theoretical ­ approach a for sustainability ­ (theory b , ­ model c , ­ framework d , ­ instrument e , method, checklist, process, strategy, conceptual- izations, development, pilot test and/or ­ tool f ) • Were within a healthcare ­ setting g • Evaluated the sustainability of an EBI (Note that inconsistent terminology for EBI is prominent and thus may be referred to as a QI intervention/ initia- tive in the literature).
elements.reason: Table 1 explicitly lists study characteristics used to determine eligibility including publication type (peer-review), study design (primary research with explicit design and data collection methods), requirement for an explicit theoretical approach, healthcare setting, and that studies evaluated sustainability of an EBI.

elements.quote: We only included published studies in the English language and peer-reviewed primary studies in this review. This review entailed a comprehensive search of published literature and rigorous review methods; however, we recognize that there is the possibility of incomplete retrieval of identified research. For example, all gray literature was excluded.
elements.reason: The review specifies language (English) and publication/report status (published, peer-reviewed primary studies; gray literature excluded) but does not report any dissemination year limits; therefore eligibility criteria for report characteristics are only partially specified.
No explicit statement distinguishes excluding studies because outcomes were not measured from excluding studies because outcome results were not reported in the provided evidence.
The evidence does not specify groups used in each synthesis nor link groups to comparisons defined in the review objectives; no synthesis groupings are described in the provided material.
Although notable restrictions (e.g., English language, peer-reviewed only, exclusion of gray literature) are stated, the evidence does not provide rationales explaining these notable restrictions.

elements.quote: In December 2018 and July 2020, we searched the following databases: Ovid MEDLINE(R) and Epub Ahead of Print, In-Process and Other Non-Indexed Citations and Daily (1946 to current); OVID Embase (1974 to current); EBSCOhost CINAHL Plus with Full-text (1937 to current); Wiley Cochrane Library (inception to current).
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports the dates when searches were conducted (December 2018 and July 2020).

elements.quote: we searched the following databases: Ovid MEDLINE(R) and Epub Ahead of Print, In-Process and Other Non-Indexed Citations and Daily (1946 to current); OVID Embase (1974 to current); EBSCOhost CINAHL Plus with Full-text (1937 to current); Wiley Cochrane Library (inception to current).
elements.reason: The manuscript names each bibliographic database, indicates the platform/interface (e.g., Ovid, OVID Embase, EBSCOhost, Wiley Cochrane Library) and reports coverage dates for each database.
No evidence that study registers, regulatory databases, or online repositories were searched; the manuscript only reports searches of bibliographic databases.
No evidence that websites, search engines, or other online sources (with names/URLs) were searched; only bibliographic databases are listed.
No evidence that organisations or manufacturers were contacted to identify studies.
No evidence describing types of individuals contacted to identify studies.
No evidence specifying the types of reference lists examined.
No evidence of backward or forward citation searching (no seed reports, citation index/platform, or search date reported).
No evidence that journals or conference proceedings were specifically consulted (no names, dates covered, or search methods reported).

elements.quote: Additional file 1. Search strategy. The four databases searched on Dec 21, 2018, as well as an additional search in July 2020. The file depicts the date of searchers and strategy used, including all search terms in each database.
elements.reason: The record states that the complete search strategy with dates and all search terms for each database is provided in Additional file 1 (supplementary material), indicating the full search strategies are reported (though in supplementary files).

elements.quote: We only included published studies in the English language and peer-reviewed primary studies in this review. This review entailed a comprehensive search of published literature and rigorous review methods; however, we recognize that there is the possibility of incomplete retrieval of identified research. For example, all gray literature was excluded.
elements.reason: Language and gray literature limits are reported (English-only; exclusion of gray literature). However, while limits are described, explicit justification of these limits by direct reference to the eligibility criteria is not provided in the retrieved evidence (only the limits and inclusion/exclusion criteria are stated).
No citation or description of published search approaches or filters, nor any adaptations, is present in the provided evidence.
No information about use of natural-language processing or text-analysis tools to identify or refine search terms is present in the provided evidence.
No information about tools used to translate search strings between sources is reported in the provided evidence.
No description of any validation of the search strategy, validation process, or validation studies is present in the provided evidence.
No description of peer review of the search strategy (e.g., PRESS) or the process/tool used is present in the retrieved evidence.
No information describing the final conceptual search structure or explorations used to develop it when not based on PICO is present in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: In the first screening stage, one reviewer (RF) independently screened the abstracts and titles of all the citations retrieved from the database searches. A second reviewer (AB) independently screened a randomly selected 10% of all titles and abstracts to verify selection for inclusion or exclusion. In the second stage, two reviewers (RF and AB) independently screened all full-text articles that had passed first-stage screening.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports the number of reviewers at each stage: one primary screener for all titles/abstracts with a second reviewer checking 10%, and two reviewers independently screening all full texts.

elements.quote: one reviewer (RF) independently screened the abstracts and titles... A second reviewer (AB) independently screened a randomly selected 10%... In the second stage, two reviewers (RF and AB) independently screened all full-text articles
elements.reason: The text explicitly states that reviewers screened independently at both the title/abstract stage and the full-text stage.

elements.quote: We discussed any differences in screening at team meetings and refined our inclusion and exclusion criteria to reflect these discussions.
elements.reason: The authors describe resolving screening disagreements via discussion at team meetings and refining criteria based on those discussions.
No evidence in the provided text that processes were used to obtain or confirm eligibility information from study investigators; the manuscript does not report contacting investigators.
No methods for translating abstracts or full articles are reported; the review also states only English-language studies were included, indicating translation was not used.
No description of integration of automation tools into the selection process is provided. EndNote X7 is mentioned as a management system but no automation for selection is described.
There is no mention of externally derived classifiers, their versions/references, roles, or records removed before screening in the flow diagram in the provided evidence.
No information is reported about internally derived classifiers, their training, validation, or use in screening.
No machine-learning prioritisation tools or screening stopping/prioritisation rules are described in the provided evidence.
There is no mention of crowdsourcing platforms or their integration into study selection in the provided materials.
The manuscript does not describe use of previously screened datasets to eliminate records; no such datasets or derivation methods are reported in the evidence provided.

elements.quote: The two reviewers independently extracted the following variables: (1) study design, (2) evaluation type (independent versus composite), (3) sustainability definition and terms used, (4) type and name of theoretical approach, (5) purpose of approach use, (6) data collection methods, (7) timing of evaluation data collection (e.g., pre-, and/or post-implementation of intervention), (8) reported sustainability measures and, 9. reported sustainability outcomes.
elements.reason: Explicitly states that two reviewers extracted data, reporting the number of reviewers collecting data from each report.

elements.quote: The two reviewers independently extracted the following variables: ...
elements.reason: Specifies that the two reviewers worked independently during data extraction.

elements.quote: We discussed any differences in screening at team meetings and refined our inclusion and exclusion criteria to reflect these discussions.
elements.reason: Describes a process (discussion at team meetings) used to resolve differences arising during screening, indicating how disagreements were handled.
No description found about processes to obtain or confirm data from study investigators in the provided evidence.
No information provided about the use, training, or validation of automation tools for data collection.
No methods for translating articles for data collection are reported in the available evidence.
No specification of software used to extract data from figures is present in the provided evidence.
No decision rules for selecting data from multiple reports or resolving inconsistencies are described in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: We extracted whether an included study evaluated (a) sustainability determinants and (b) sustainability outcomes and how they measured these variables. We defined sustainability determinants as correlates and predictors of sustainability (organizational, contextual, and strategies) and sustainability outcomes as the subsequent impact (healthcare improvement or public health outcomes) of sustained intervention use [5]. To further unpack sustainability outcomes, we extracted and synthesized nine sustainability outcomes across the 64 included studies (Table 3) [6, 15, 16].
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists and defines outcome domains (sustainability determinants and sustainability outcomes) and states that nine sustainability outcomes were extracted and synthesized.

elements.quote: Of 64 included studies, 66% ( n = 43) ... had a clear timing for evaluation and 33% ( n = 21) ... had unclear timing. Of the 43 studies with clear timing, 42% ( n = 18) evaluated sustainability at a single time point ... The remaining 57% ( n = 25) evaluated sustainability at multiple time points ... The majority of studies (63%; n = 40) conducted data collection post evaluation only ... Evaluation timing and data collection time points are provided in Table 9.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports overall measurement timing (e.g., single vs multiple time points, pre/post) for included studies, but does not specify the time frame of measurement for each individual outcome domain.
No statement was found indicating whether all results compatible with each outcome domain (e.g., all measures, time points, analyses) were sought.
There is no description of a process used to select results when not all compatible results were sought; the manuscript does not report such a selection process.
No evidence was found reporting changes to outcome-domain inclusion, definitions, or importance with rationales.
No evidence was found reporting changes to processes for selecting results within eligible outcome domains with rationales.
The manuscript does not report which outcomes were considered most important for interpreting conclusions nor provide a rationale for any prioritisation.

elements.quote: The two reviewers independently extracted the following variables: (1) study design, (2) evaluation type (independent versus composite), (3) sustainability definition and terms used, (4) type and name of theoretical approach, (5) purpose of approach use, (6) data collection methods, (7) timing of evaluation data collection (e.g., pre-, and/or post-implementation of intervention), (8) reported sustainability measures and, 9. reported sustainability outcomes.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists the additional variables extracted for each study (nine items including study design, evaluation type, sustainability definitions, theoretical approach, data collection methods, timing, measures, and outcomes).
No text in the provided evidence describes assumptions made about missing or unclear study information.

No explicit citation or mention is provided of a tool used to determine which data items to collect (e.g., a piloted data extraction form, a standardized checklist, or similar) in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: We used the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) [17] to assess the methodological quality of studies.
elements.reason: The specific risk-of-bias tool (MMAT) is explicitly named, but no version number or publication year of the MMAT is reported in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: The MMAT [17] appraises the quality by study design type, such as quantitative, qualitative, or mixed empirical methods. We distinguished mixed-methods as studies combining both qualitative and quantitative methods, whereas studies classified as multi-methods used 2 + qualitative methods. The criteria are specific to each type of study, with five domains apportioned to qualitative studies and quantitative studies subdivided into randomized controlled, non-randomized and descriptive studies.
elements.reason: The domains/components assessed by the MMAT are described (design-specific criteria, five domains for qualitative, and subdivisions for quantitative study types).

elements.quote: Each study is assigned an overall quality score, using asterisks representing the quality appraisal of each study. Scores vary from 20% (*) when one criterion is met to 100% (*****) when all criteria are met.
elements.reason: An overall risk-of-bias/quality judgement (an overall quality score expressed with asterisks and percentage equivalents) is reported, including the scoring rules linking number of criteria met to percentage/asterisk ratings.
No information is provided in the retrieved evidence about any adaptations made to the MMAT or other risk-of-bias tools.
The review used an existing tool (MMAT); there is no indication that a newly developed risk-of-bias tool was created for this study.

elements.quote: Two reviewers independently completed MMAT assessments and compared scoring.
elements.reason: The number of reviewers and that they worked independently is reported. However, a detailed disagreement-resolution procedure (e.g., third reviewer adjudication or predefined consensus process) is not described beyond stating that they compared scoring.
No processes for obtaining or confirming risk-of-bias information from study investigators are described in the provided evidence.
There is no mention of any automation tools being used for risk-of-bias assessment in the retrieved evidence.

No text in the provided evidence specifies effect measures (e.g., risk ratio, mean difference) for any outcome or outcome type. The Methods and Data Synthesis sections describe integrative review methods and data extraction but do not report effect measures.
No thresholds or ranges for interpreting effect sizes, nor any rationale for such thresholds, are reported in the provided evidence.
The evidence does not describe any methods used to re-express synthesized results using another effect measure.
There is no justification reported for the choice of any effect measure in the provided Methods or Results excerpts.

elements.quote: We used Endnote X7 as the management system for this review. After removing duplicates, we conducted a two-stage screening process of the citations retrieved from our database searches. In the first screening stage, one reviewer (RF) independently screened the abstracts and titles of all the citations retrieved from the database searches. A second reviewer (AB) independently screened a randomly selected 10% of all titles and abstracts to verify selection for inclusion or exclusion. In the second stage, two reviewers (RF and AB) independently screened all full-text articles that had passed first-stage screening. We discussed any differences in screening at team meetings and refined our inclusion and exclusion criteria to reflect these discussions.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the screening process and how inclusion/exclusion decisions were made (two-stage screening, independent reviewers, discussion and refinement of criteria), but does not explicitly describe the processes used to decide which studies were eligible for each synthesis (for example, how studies were tabulated or compared against planned groups for specific syntheses).

No retrieved evidence describes methods used to prepare data for presentation or synthesis (e.g., handling of missing summary statistics, data conversions). The provided sections cover screening, data extraction variables (text_10), use of EndNote and screening流程 (text_9), and general data analysis approach (text_8), but none specify procedures for preparing or converting extracted data or handling missing summary statistics.

elements.quote: Evidence tables were created to summarize and describe the studies included in this review.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states that evidence tables were created to summarize and describe included studies; additionally, Table 4 (chunk_id table_2) shows a tabular structure used to display study data (data collection methods and referenced studies).

elements.quote: Our synthesis indicated that there is a breadth of theoretical approaches and constructs that were considered for the evaluation of the sustainability of EBIs in healthcare that were consistent with other recent synthesis work [6-10]. A recent scoping review and theory analysis [8] found 37 sustainability determinant factors, which grouped into seven themes: (1) characteristics of the innovation / EBP; (2) adopter/user factors influencing sustained use (3) leadership and management influences/factors; (4) inner context (practice setting/organization) factors where EBPs are delivered; (5) inner processes / infrastructure factors that support the EBPs (e.g., processes, methods, systems, structures, or strategies); (6) outer context or broader system factors; and (7) outcomes descriptions without defined factors. These themes are similar to the work of Lennox et al. Most sustainability evaluations included in this study used qualitative research designs (48%), with interviews as the most common data collection method. This finding is consistent with the work of Lennox [6] who reported 59% of their included studies used qualitative methods.
elements.reason: The discussion explicitly compares the review's findings to other syntheses (citing Lennox et al. and a recent scoping review), noting consistencies in themes and methods, thereby interpreting results in the context of existing evidence.
